title: How do you build a training matrix for a hospital?
description: How to build a hospital training matrix: clinical and support roles against CMS, Joint Commission, OSHA, HIPAA, NSQHS and Ahpra duties, with refresh clocks.
shortAnswer: A hospital training matrix is built by listing clinical and support roles against every obligation that applies in the hospital's market, such as the CMS Conditions of Participation, OSHA and HIPAA in the United States, or the NSQHS Standards and Ahpra registration standards in Australia, then recording for each cell the frequency, the trigger and the evidence that proves competence rather than attendance.
keyTakeaways: Hospital obligations come in three layers: funding or accreditation conditions, workplace safety law, and individual professional registration. Each row should name its layer and its market.
Frequencies do not line up. CMS emergency preparedness runs every 2 years, OSHA bloodborne pathogens annually, and CLIA competency twice in the first year and then annually.
Several hospital rules ask staff to demonstrate knowledge or competence, so a completion record alone will not satisfy those cells.
Professional development and credentialing belong to the practitioner and the credentialing committee, but the hospital still needs a row that verifies them.
Retention periods range from 1 year to 7 years across the rules covered here, so set retention per row, not one policy for the whole matrix.

sections.heading: Which obligations feed a hospital training matrix?

blocks.text: A hospital matrix draws on three layers: conditions attached to funding or accreditation, workplace safety law, and the registration duties of individual clinicians. The layer matters because it decides who owns the requirement and what a surveyor or auditor will ask to see. This guide applies the general method in [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) to hospitals in the United States and Australia, using only obligations documented in this library's regulation pages.
**United States.** For hospitals that participate in Medicare and Medicaid, the main sources are:

items: The CMS hospital Conditions of Participation in 42 CFR Part 482, which contain separate training duties for emergency preparedness, restraint and seclusion, infection prevention and control, discharge transfer protocols and emergency services readiness ([CMS hospital Conditions of Participation](/regulations/cms-hospital-conditions-of-participation-training)).

Joint Commission accreditation, where requirements above the Conditions of Participation have sat in National Performance Goals since January 1, 2026, including goals on staff competence and on waived testing ([Joint Commission staff competency](/regulations/joint-commission-staff-competency-requirements)).

The Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) for anyone who tests patient specimens at moderate or high complexity ([CLIA competency](/regulations/clia-laboratory-personnel-competency-requirements)).

Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) standards for staff exposed to blood or required to wear respirators ([bloodborne pathogens](/regulations/osha-bloodborne-pathogens-training-requirements); [respiratory protection](/regulations/osha-respiratory-protection-training-requirements)).

Office for Civil Rights rules on HIPAA privacy and security training and on Section 1557 civil rights training ([HIPAA](/regulations/hipaa-security-and-privacy-training); [Section 1557](/regulations/section-1557-nondiscrimination-training-requirements)).

Where the hospital system also runs a Medicare Advantage or Part D plan, the sponsor's compliance and fraud, waste and abuse training ([Medicare compliance program training](/regulations/cms-medicare-compliance-program-training-requirements)).

In California, the workplace violence prevention framework. Health care settings have their own Cal/OSHA standard, title 8 section 3342, listed separately from the general industry rule, so a hospital should confirm which standard covers each site before writing that row ([California workplace violence prevention](/regulations/california-workplace-violence-prevention-training)).

blocks.text: **Australia.** All public and private hospitals must be accredited to the National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS) Standards ([NSQHS workforce training](/regulations/nsqhs-standards-workforce-training)). Alongside the Standards sit credentialing and scope of practice ([credentialing](/regulations/credentialing-and-scope-of-clinical-practice-australia)), continuing professional development set by the National Boards ([Ahpra CPD](/regulations/ahpra-cpd-registration-standards); [pharmacist CPD](/regulations/pharmacist-cpd-requirements-australia)), radiation use licensing, shown here for New South Wales ([radiation user licensing](/regulations/radiation-safety-licence-training-australia)), and state child abuse reporting duties ([mandatory reporting](/regulations/mandatory-reporting-training-australia)).

sections.heading: Which hospital roles need their own rows?

blocks.text: Split roles wherever the obligations differ, even if the job title is shared. In a hospital, a registered nurse in the emergency department and a registered nurse in day surgery may carry different restraint, emergency readiness and point of care testing duties. The role list below is a practical starting point.

items: **Bedside nursing staff**, split by unit where restraint, emergency readiness or waived testing duties apply.

**Medical staff and licensed practitioners**, including those who order restraint or seclusion, which needs working knowledge of hospital policy under 482.13(e)(11), and specialists who use fluoroscopy.
**Laboratory testing personnel**, split by test complexity because CLIA competency rules apply to moderate and high complexity testing but not to waived-only laboratories.
**Pharmacists**, whose CPD runs on credits rather than hours in Australia.
**Environmental services and cleaning staff**, who appear in NSQHS cleaning training actions and usually in OSHA bloodborne pathogens scope.
**Registration, health information and billing staff**, who are workforce members for HIPAA and often relevant employees for Section 1557.
**Volunteers, students, agency and contracted staff**, who are named in CMS emergency preparedness training and in NSQHS orientation (Action 1.19).
**Governing body members and executives**, who appear in NSQHS orientation and, for plan sponsors, in CMS compliance training.

blocks.text: Grouping by [role based training](/glossary/role-based-training) rather than by person means a nurse who transfers from day surgery to the emergency department inherits the new rows on the day of transfer.

blocks.text: Notice that the Australian row needs a license check, not a course. In NSW, a specialist using fluoroscopy generally needs AHPRA specialist registration plus an approved fluoroscopy course to obtain the license, and licenses are valid for 1 or 3 years, so the matrix tracks expiry rather than a training refresh.

sections.heading: Why do hospital refresh clocks need careful wording?

blocks.text: Because the rules phrase their clocks differently, and a matrix that rounds them all to 'annual' will be wrong in both directions. Write each clock exactly as the source states it, then let the system calculate due dates. The general approach is in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

items: **Within one year of the previous session.** OSHA bloodborne pathogens training is due within one year of the last session, so a fixed calendar month for everyone does not satisfy it.
**At least every 2 years.** CMS emergency preparedness training is biennial, but new training is also due after significant plan updates.
**Semiannual, then annual.** CLIA competency is evaluated at least twice in a tester's first year, then at least annually.

**Annual with a fixed period.** Pharmacists in Australia need 40 CPD credits in each 12 month period ending 30 September, and doctors 50 hours per calendar year, so the period does not match the hospital's financial or hire date year.
**Not annual at all.** HIPAA privacy training is required for new workforce members within a reasonable period and after material policy changes, with no annual frequency in the current rule.

**Event driven.** CLIA requires reevaluation before reporting results after a methodology or instrument change, and NSQHS Action 1.23 requires scope of practice review when a new service, procedure or technology is introduced.

sections.heading: What evidence and retention should each hospital row carry?

blocks.text: Each row should state its evidence type and its retention period, because both vary by source. Several hospital rules ask for demonstrated knowledge or competence, and Joint Commission's standards interpretation says a self-assessment such as a skills checklist, used as the sole method, does not constitute competency assessment. Those rows need an observed or tested assessment, as described in [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment).

blocks.text: Set the longest period that applies to a record where one course serves several rows. A combined induction that covers bloodborne pathogens and HIPAA, for example, sits under the 6 year HIPAA rule. The method for setting these periods is in [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How should CPD and credentialing appear on the matrix?

blocks.text: As verification rows, not delivery rows. In Australia, CPD is the registered practitioner's obligation under section 128 of the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law, and the practitioner declares it at renewal. The hospital's row checks that registration is current, which a listing on the national register proves; the Nursing and Midwifery Board points employers to the Practitioner Information Exchange service for bulk checks.

Credentialing works the same way. NSQHS Action 1.24 requires processes to ensure clinicians are credentialed where relevant, and the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care's May 2026 guidance describes re-credentialing every 3 to 5 years as specified by the jurisdiction, completed before expiry, with temporary credentialing generally valid for up to three months. A matrix row for each credentialed clinician should carry the credential expiry, the approved scope, and a flag when a new procedure or technology changes that scope.

sections.heading: Which hospital rules are changing in 2026 and 2027?

blocks.text: Several rows will change within the next two years, so give each one an owner who watches the source. As at November 2026, the library's regulation pages record these pending changes:

items: **Maternal care training (US).** 42 CFR 482.59(c) takes effect January 1, 2027, with initial training for new staff and biennial training for staff the governing body identifies.

**HIPAA Security Rule (US).** A January 2025 proposed rule would require security awareness training at least every 12 months and within 30 days of access for new members. No final rule was found as at September 2026, so the current rule still governs.
**California workplace violence (US, California).** The Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board is required to adopt a general industry standard by December 31, 2026.
**NSQHS Standards third edition (Australia).** A pilot is planned for 2027, final release for 2028, and assessment from 2030; services continue using the second edition meanwhile.
**Ahpra CPD standards (Australia).** Fourteen National Boards consulted on revised CPD standards between May and July 2026; the draft proposes 20 hours including 5 interactive.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each hospital matrix row against its source clause, market, clock and evidence rule, so a change such as a new Condition of Participation flags the affected roles and assessments. See [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences) and [audit evidence](/platform/audit-evidence).

faqs.q: Does Joint Commission accreditation replace the CMS Conditions of Participation in the matrix?
faqs.a: No. Joint Commission's Accreditation 360 manual identifies the CMS Conditions of Participation and its own National Performance Goals separately, and the goals sit on top of the federal conditions. Keep both as rows, and mark where one assessment satisfies both so staff are not trained twice on the same content.

faqs.q: Do waived testing staff need CLIA competency assessment?
faqs.a: Not under federal CLIA rules. CMS states that laboratories performing only waived tests are not required to assess testing personnel competency. Joint Commission accredited hospitals still need waived testing competence assessed at orientation and annually under National Performance Goal 10, so the row remains, with Joint Commission as its source.

faqs.q: Can mandatory CPR or fire training count toward a nurse's CPD in Australia?
faqs.a: No. The Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia states that routine annual CPR and mandatory fire training cannot be counted toward CPD hours. Keep them as hospital mandatory training rows, separate from the CPD verification row, so neither status hides a gap in the other.

faqs.q: Should contractors and agency staff appear on a hospital matrix?
faqs.a: Yes. CMS emergency preparedness training covers individuals providing services under arrangement and volunteers, infection control training covers contracted personnel as applicable, and NSQHS Action 1.19 names locum, agency, student and volunteer members. Assign them to roles like employees, with evidence obtained from the agency where it delivers the training.
